title: Under the Southern Cross
caption: The Southern Cross over the Danish 1.54-meter telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at La Silla Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The Danish 1.54-meter telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory looks out at the southern sky with its dome open. To the left of the dome, set in the plane of the Milky Way, is the Southern Cross, one of the most distinctive star patterns in the sky.

The Cross is formed by Alpha, Beta, Gamma and Delta Crucis, four stars of the constellation Crux. They are not neighbors in space. The nearest, Gamma Crucis, is just 88 light-years from Earth, while the most distant is 364 light-years away. Alpha Crucis, a blue-white star at the bottom of the Cross, ranks as the 13th brightest star anywhere in the night sky.
Just above the Cross lies a dark smudge, the Coalsack Nebula. It is a cloud of interstellar dust that blocks the light of stars behind it, leaving what looks like an empty patch in the Milky Way.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at an ESO site, in visible light. The camera settings and color processing are not published.
understand.eye: The Coalsack is visible to the naked eye, but a long camera exposure gathers much more light, bringing out the red nebulae and the density of Milky Way stars.

explore: Below the Cross are two patches of glowing gas, the red emission nebula IC 2948 and the Carina Nebula. The photo comes from the Ultra High Definition Expedition to La Silla.
alt: A telescope dome with its slit open under the Milky Way, with the Southern Cross to the left, a dark dust patch above it and reddish nebulae below.
